business.title: Ultralow-volume shallow microwell-based collection and processing for scalable spatial proteome mapping of tissues
business.description: Multi-ome mapping technologies for precise comprehensive characterization of tissues at high spatial resolutions are crucial for providing insights into tissue heterogeneity and microenvironment within spatial context. However, proteome mapping technologies lag far behind other transcriptome (genome) mapping technologies. Here we report an Ultralow-volume, Shallow, Microwell plate-based voxel Collection and Processing coupled with mass spectrometry (MS) method, termed USMCP-MS, for robust scalable proteome mapping of tissues at high spatial resolutions. This method was built upon the design of an ultralow-volume, shallow 96-well plate for robust rapid collection and processing of single voxels. Using a commonly accessible MS platform, USMCP-MS enables reproducible label-free quantification of ~1,700 and ~2,500 protein groups from single voxels of fresh frozen mouse brain tissue at 20 µm × 20 µm × 10 µm ( ~ 1 cell region) and 50 µm × 50 µm × 10 µm ( ~ 6 cell region), respectively. More importantly, USMCP-MS can be broadly applied to different types of tissues (fresh frozen, OCT-embedded, and FFPE) for 2D proteome mapping of region areas of interest at 50–100 µm spatial resolutions, revealing spatially resolved protein signatures and region-specific signaling pathways. With its further improvement, USMCP-MS may pave the way for routine, robust, scalable proteome mapping of tissues at single-cell spatial resolution. Spatial proteome mapping is essential for understanding tissue heterogeneity and microenvironment. Here, authors report USMCP-MS, a robust, scalable, unbiased spatial proteomics method for proteome mapping of tissues at high spatial resolutions as well as high-throughput single voxel proteomics.

science.title: Quasi-degenerate cation occupation enables oxygen-vacancy defect healing in nonlinear optical crystals
science.description: Chemical substitution is an effective strategy to enhance the desired performances of materials based on known structural prototypes. However, it almost invariably introduces intrinsic defects, such as vacancies and twinning defects, which couple with dopants and obscure or degrade the intrinsic properties. Therefore, chemical substitution that enables atomically precise engineering of materials without generating defect structures remains challenging. Here, we propose a quasi-degenerate cation occupation strategy to overcome this detrimental coupling and successfully apply it to the langasite-family nonlinear optical (NLO) crystal, La3TiGa5O14 (LGTi). Therein, the cross-site occupation of Ti and Ti3+/Ti4+ redox flexibility improves the kinetic accessibility of oxygen-vacancy (VO) defects associated with cation disorder, enabling their removal during oxidative annealing. The oxidized LGTi single crystal has a VO-related defect concentration below the electron paramagnetic resonance detection limit, with a laser damage threshold of 2.53 GW/cm2 and a large NLO coefficient of 3.51 pm/V, both exceeding the previously reported values for bulk langasite-family crystals. Overall, this work provides a quasi-degenerate cation occupation strategy to mitigate substitution-induced defects in structurally complex crystalline systems and has great prospects in enhancing material performance. A quasi-degenerate cation occupation strategy offers a pathway to overcome substitution-induced defects in functional crystals. Its validation in La3TiGa5O14 demonstrates effective oxygen-vacancy healing and improved nonlinear optical performance.

science.title: Harnessing plant cells as oral drug delivery capsules for synergistic therapy of ulcerative colitis
science.description: Cell-derived carriers are important excipients in drug delivery systems; however, most studies have focused on mammalian cells. Plant cells, by comparison, offer intrinsic therapeutic potential and feature a bilayer structure composed of cell wall and cell membrane. Here, we utilize the carrot plant cells as oral colon-targeting drug delivery vehicles leveraging their intrinsic therapeutic properties and the outer layer of cell wall. Utilizing ulcerative colitis and glucocorticoid budesonide as a disease and drug model, the drug loading strategy, colon microenvironment sensitivity, colon-specific drug release and anti-inflammation efficacies of the plant cell-based delivery system are evaluated. In particular, the budesonide-loaded liposomes are linked to carrot cells via click chemistry to achieve budesonide-loaded carrot cells, which are validated to maintain stable and decrease the drug distribution and absorption in stomach and small intestine, while disintegrated by local microbiota after reaching colon to allow colon-targeting release. The glucocorticoid drug, intrinsic anti-inflammation substances in plant cells and the short-chain fatty acids generated by cell wall enzymatic degradation work synergistically to strengthen the therapeutic efficacy in ulcerative colitis mice models. This work provides insights into the development of plant-based drug excipients and offers an alternative strategy for the targeted treatment of colonic diseases. Plant cells have been explored as carriers for drug delivery through genetic engineering. Here, the authors report a plant cell-based oral colon-targeted delivery system that links drug-loaded, maleimide-modified liposomes to carrot cells through maleimide-thiol click chemistry.

science.title: An explainable machine learning framework for soil susceptibility mapping using SHapley additive exPlanation
science.description: Soil salinity and alkalinity are among the most critical land degradation processes that threaten agricultural productivity, ecosystem stability, and sustainable soil management. However, accurate modeling, especially over large areas, remains challenging due to the limited spatial and temporal coverage of soil samples, the quality of predictor variables, and the choice of modeling algorithm. To address these limitations, this study used “machine learning (ML)” and “explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)” to map combined soil hazards based on soil pH and electrical conductivity (EC) (0–30 cm depth) in the Qarah-Aghaj River basin, Fars Province, Iran. By integrating pH and EC measurements from 72 soil samples ​with climatic, anthropogenic, soil, hydrological, and topographic predictors, we modeled the spatial distribution of soil pH and EC. “Random Forest (RF)” and “Support Vector Regression (SVR)” were introduced for prediction, as RF outperformed SVR for both EC and pH prediction, achieving higher predictive accuracy (R2 > 0.75) and lower error values across the validation datasets. “SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)” was applied separately to the EC and pH models to interpret the contribution of predictor variables at both low and high values of the target properties. The results of the combined soil hazard map revealed that 94.41% of the study area was affected by only alkalinity hazards and 1.26% of the total area faced both alkalinity and salinity hazards. These findings offer a valuable tool for regional and environmental planning and sustainable soil management. This study also emphasizes the need to carefully evaluate covariate selection strategies and modeling approaches, as their effectiveness can vary depending on the algorithm and data characteristics.
